label: Policy vs standard vs procedure vs guideline

mentor.diagnosis: You picked the wrong level of the governance hierarchy. All four documents are real, and the exam decides between them on how specific the document is and whether following it is optional.
contrast: All access must be authenticated and authorised
Passwords must be at least 14 characters
How to do it, step by step
The onboarding checklist, the incident playbook
Suggested practices for choosing a passphrase
mentor.rule: Policy is the why, standard is the what, procedure is the how, guideline is the suggestion. Only the guideline is optional.
mentor.tell: A specific measurable value such as a key length or a password length is a standard. Numbered steps are a procedure. The word 'should' or 'recommended' signals a guideline.
mentor.trap: Policy is the broadest term and is loosely used for all four in everyday speech, so it feels safe. The exam uses the hierarchy strictly.

label: Data owner vs controller vs processor vs custodian or steward

mentor.diagnosis: You assigned the wrong role. These are separated by who decides, who acts on instructions, and who keeps the systems running.
contrast: Accountable for the data: classification and who may access it
A senior business leader, such as the head of HR
Decides the purpose and means of processing
The organisation itself, in privacy law
Processes data on the controller's instructions
A payroll bureau or cloud provider
Implements and maintains the controls day to day
The living person the data is about
mentor.rule: Owner is accountable, custodian is operational, controller decides the purpose, processor follows instructions.
mentor.tell: 'Decides why and how the data is used' is the controller. 'Runs the backups and applies the permissions' is the custodian. 'Sets the classification' is the owner.
mentor.trap: Owner and controller sound interchangeable in plain English. Owner is the internal accountability role, controller is the privacy law role, and the exam uses both.

label: SLA vs MOU vs MOA vs MSA vs SOW vs NDA vs BPA

mentor.diagnosis: You matched on a vague sense of 'contract' rather than on what each document actually fixes.
contrast: Measurable service levels: uptime, response time, penalties
A shared understanding of intent between parties
Agreed roles and responsibilities, more formal than an MOU
The umbrella terms governing an ongoing relationship
The specific deliverables and timeline for one piece of work
How two businesses will operate a joint venture, including profit sharing
mentor.rule: MSA is the umbrella, SOW is the individual job under it. SLA is the measurable promise. MOU is intent without teeth.
mentor.tell: Any number with a unit, such as 99.9% or four hours, means SLA. 'Deliverables and milestones for this project' means SOW.
mentor.trap: MOU and MOA differ by one letter and are both about mutual understanding. MOU is intent, MOA adds defined responsibilities and is normally binding.

label: Transfer vs accept vs avoid vs mitigate

mentor.diagnosis: You named a treatment that does not match what the organisation actually did with the risk.
contrast: Deploy MFA to reduce credential theft
Financial impact moved to a third party
Buy cyber insurance, or outsource the function
The activity is stopped, so the risk no longer exists
Cancel the product line that required storing card data
Acknowledged and nothing further is done
Documented as an exception, signed off by the risk owner
mentor.rule: Avoid removes the activity. Mitigate reduces the risk. Transfer moves who pays. Accept does nothing but write it down.
mentor.tell: Insurance is always transfer. Discontinuing the service is always avoid. Note that transfer moves the financial impact, not the accountability.
mentor.trap: Outsourcing feels like avoidance because the work leaves the building. The risk still exists and you remain accountable for it, so it is transfer.

mentor.diagnosis: You classified the analysis by how rigorous it felt rather than by whether it produces currency figures.
contrast: High, medium, low; a heat map
Asset values and reliable frequency data
Reputational and safety risks that resist pricing
Comparing a control's cost against the loss it prevents
False precision when the input data is guessed
mentor.rule: If the answer is a number in currency, it is quantitative. If it is a word or a colour on a matrix, it is qualitative.
mentor.tell: SLE, ARO, ALE and exposure factor are all quantitative. A 5 by 5 likelihood and impact grid is qualitative.
mentor.trap: Qualitative sounds like the weaker method, so it looks wrong. It is the right method when the impact genuinely cannot be priced.

mentor.diagnosis: You used the two as synonyms. One is investigating, the other is acting.
contrast: Reviewing a vendor's SOC 2 report and finances before signing
Patching, monitoring the vendor, reviewing access quarterly
mentor.rule: Diligence is doing your homework. Care is doing your job. Diligence comes first and is a point in time; care is ongoing.
mentor.tell: 'Before entering the agreement' or 'during vendor selection' is due diligence. 'On an ongoing basis' is due care.
mentor.trap: Both describe a responsible organisation being careful, so both read as correct. Decide by whether it happens before or after the commitment.

label: Internal audit vs external audit vs self-assessment vs attestation

mentor.diagnosis: You chose a review type without checking who performs it and how independent they must be.
contrast: The team that owns the control
An internal audit function reporting to the audit committee
Independent of the team, not of the organisation
Assurance to management and the board
Assurance to customers, partners and regulators
A signed formal statement that something is true
Evidence a control or condition holds
mentor.rule: The more independent the reviewer, the more weight the result carries outside the organisation. A customer asking for assurance will not accept your self-assessment.
mentor.tell: 'A customer requires evidence before renewing' means an independent third-party audit, not an internal one.
mentor.trap: An internal audit is genuinely independent of the team being audited, which makes it feel sufficient. It is still the organisation auditing itself.

label: Known, partially known and unknown environment testing, and passive vs active reconnaissance

mentor.diagnosis: You mixed up how much the tester was told with what the tester then did.
contrast: Tester is given full information: architecture, credentials, source
Tester is given nothing and must discover it
Gathering information without touching the target: WHOIS, OSINT, social media
Interacting with the target: scanning, enumeration, banner grabbing
mentor.rule: Known, partially known and unknown describe what the tester was told. Passive and active describe whether the target can see the tester.
mentor.tell: 'Simulates an external attacker with no inside knowledge' is unknown environment. 'Without alerting the target or touching its systems' is passive reconnaissance.
mentor.trap: Unknown environment testing usually begins with passive reconnaissance, so the two appear together and get merged. They answer different questions.

label: Right-to-audit clause vs independent assessment vs questionnaire vs supply chain analysis

mentor.diagnosis: You chose a vendor assurance method that does not give the level of confidence the scenario asked for.
contrast: The vendor's own answers about its controls
Better, still the vendor auditing itself
A third party's report, such as SOC 2
Strong, and on the vendor's schedule and scope
A contractual right for YOU to audit them
Strongest, on your schedule and your scope
Visibility into the vendor's own suppliers
mentor.rule: A right-to-audit clause must be negotiated into the contract before signing. Afterwards you get whatever the vendor chooses to share.
mentor.tell: 'We must be able to inspect their controls ourselves, at a time of our choosing' is a right-to-audit clause.
mentor.trap: A SOC 2 report is genuinely independent and is the usual answer, but its scope and timing are chosen by the vendor. When the stem stresses your control over the review, it is the right-to-audit clause.

label: Business impact analysis vs risk assessment

mentor.diagnosis: You confused the exercise that identifies threats with the one that measures what disruption costs.
contrast: What could go wrong and how likely is it
If this process stops, how bad is it and how fast must it return
A risk register with likelihood and impact
Business continuity and disaster recovery plans
mentor.rule: Risk assessment asks what might happen. BIA assumes it already happened and asks what it costs per hour.
mentor.tell: Anything producing RTO or RPO figures is a BIA. Anything producing likelihood ratings is a risk assessment.
mentor.trap: Both analyse impact, and both feed planning. The BIA is deliberately indifferent to cause, which is the cleanest way to separate them.

label: Security awareness: campaigns, reporting, and anomalous behaviour recognition

mentor.diagnosis: You answered a human behaviour problem with a technical control, or measured the wrong thing.
contrast: Targeted follow-up training for those users
Users do not report suspicious messages
A one-click report button plus recognition for reporting
Report rate and time to report, not just click rate
Recurring training, with the content refreshed
mentor.rule: A rising report rate is a better signal than a falling click rate. Someone has to click eventually; what matters is how fast you hear about it.
mentor.tell: 'Users are not reporting' means make reporting easy and rewarded. Punishing reporters guarantees silence.
mentor.trap: Click rate is the number every phishing platform puts on the dashboard, so it looks like the metric. It measures the attack, not your response capability.

label: Backout plan vs maintenance window vs impact analysis vs approval

mentor.diagnosis: You named the wrong element of the change process for what the scenario was actually missing.
contrast: Nobody realised the change would take the VPN down
Did it work somewhere safe first
It was applied straight to production
How do we undo this if it goes wrong
The change failed and the team could not revert
The change ran at 10am on a trading day
How is this kind of change normally done
mentor.rule: Match the element to the failure. Could not undo means backout plan. Wrong time means maintenance window. Unexpected side effect means impact analysis.
mentor.tell: 'The team was unable to restore service after the update failed' is a missing backout plan, every time.
mentor.trap: Approval is the element people name by reflex because it sounds like governance. Read which part of the change actually broke.
